content: The text provided is a long and detailed list of references, guidelines, and indicators related to HIV prevention, treatment, and care, as well as monitoring and evaluation frameworks. 1. The study published in Addictive Behaviors in 2005 (Volume 30, Issue 5, Pages 865–874) discusses the settings and outcomes of interventions targeting addictive behaviors. 2. The WHO's consolidated guidelines on the use of antiretroviral drugs for treating and preventing HIV infection provide comprehensive recommendations for clinical and public health practices. 3. Cowan FM et al. conducted the Regai Dzive Shiri project, a randomized trial evaluating an HIV prevention intervention for youth, with results published in AIDS in 2010 (Volume 24, Issue 16, Pages 2541–2552). 4. Doyle AM et al. assessed the long-term biological and behavioral impact of an adolescent sexual health intervention in Tanzania through a follow-up survey of the MEMA kwa Vijana Trial, published in PLOS Medicine in 2010 (Volume 7, Issue 6, e1000287). 5. Ross DA et al. evaluated the biological and behavioral outcomes of a community-randomized trial of an adolescent sexual health intervention in Tanzania, with findings published in AIDS in 2007 (Volume 21, Issue 14, Pages 1943–1955). 6. Harper CC et al. examined the effects of increased access to emergency contraception among young adolescents, as reported in Obstetrics & Gynecology in 2005 (Volume 106, Issue 3, Pages 483–491). 7. Franklin VL et al. conducted a randomized controlled trial of Sweet Talk, a text-messaging system designed to support young people with diabetes, with results published in Diabetic Medicine in 2006 (Volume 23, Issue 12, Pages 1332–1338). 8. Chernick LS et al. explored strategies to enhance the referral of sexually active adolescent females from emergency departments to family planning services, as detailed in Journal of Women’s Health in 2015 (Volume 24, Issue 4, Pages 324–328). 9. Elliott L et al. investigated whether untargeted sexual health promotion for young people has reached its limit through a quasi-experimental study, published in Journal of Epidemiology & Community Health in 2013 (Volume 67, Issue 5, Pages 398–404). 10. Funck-Brentano I et al. evaluated the effectiveness of peer support group therapy for HIV-infected adolescents, with findings published in AIDS in 2005 (Volume 19, Issue 14, Pages 1501–1508). 11. Gilmer TP et al. analyzed changes in mental health service utilization after offering youth-specific versus adult programs for transition-age youths, as reported in Psychiatric Services in 2012 (Volume 63, Issue 6, Pages 592–596). 12. Ngo AD et al. evaluated a peer-based education project integrating HIV and sexual and reproductive health services for young people in Vietnam, with results published in PLOS One in 2013 (Volume 8, Issue 11, e80951). 13. Olson AL et al. described the Healthy Teens Counseling Approach, which aims to change adolescent health behaviors, as detailed in American Journal of Preventive Medicine in 2008 (Volume 35, Supplement 5, Pages S359–S364). 14. Teasdale CA et al. assessed the impact of youth-friendly services on the retention of 10–24-year-olds in HIV care and treatment programs in Kenya, as published in Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes in 2016 (Volume 71, Issue 2, Pages e56–e59). 15. Davila JA et al. demonstrated that centralizing HIV services for HIV-positive African-American and Hispanic youth improves retention in care, as reported in AIDS Care in 2013 (Volume 25, Issue 2, Pages 202–206). 16. Deogan C et al. estimated the resource needs for adolescent-friendly health services in 74 lowand middle-income countries, with findings published in PLOS One in 2012 (Volume 7, Issue 12, e51420). 17. Kempers J et al. conducted a cost analysis and exploratory cost-effectiveness study of youth-friendly sexual and reproductive health services in Moldova, as detailed in BMC Health Services Research in 2014 (Volume 14, Article 316). 18. Mark D et al. performed a situational analysis on the availability of appropriate HIV treatment and care services for adolescents in sub-Saharan Africa, conducted in September 2014 and accessed in February 2016. 19. Bernays S et al. summarized findings from the ARROW and BREATHER qualitative research projects addressing PICO questions for young people living with HIV, conducted in Uganda, Zimbabwe, the USA, the UK, and Ireland, in May 2015. 20. Wolmarans L et al. surveyed national HIV program managers to understand their perspectives on implementing interventions for treating and preventing HIV infection, contributing to the WHO's consolidated guidelines on antiretroviral drug use in 2015. 21. WHO's global strategy on people-centered and integrated health services emphasizes the importance of modern quality improvement approaches to strengthen health systems, as outlined in International Journal for Quality in Health Care in 2014 (Volume 26, Issue 2, Pages 117–123). 22. The WHO and US CDC collaborated to improve the quality of HIV-related point-of-care testing, ensuring the reliability and accuracy of test results, as detailed in a handbook accessed in January 2016. 23. The 2015 WHO Consolidated Strategic Information Guidelines for HIV in the Health Sector provide comprehensive guidance on monitoring national and global health sector responses to HIV, including the use of antiretroviral drugs for treatment and prevention. 24. The guidelines propose 50 national indicators, including 10 global indicators, to monitor and evaluate HIV program performance and assess its impact along the cascade of prevention, treatment, and care. 25. The 10 global indicators represent the minimum set of information needed for global reporting and provide a common platform for monitoring and comparison among countries.
